sn55.53:1.2: Despite his evident eminence, this is the only appearance of the layman Dhammadinna. For the nun of the same name, see MN 44. | Other lay followers with similarly large retinues include Anāthapiṇḍika AN 5.176:1.1, Hatthaka of Āḷavī (AN 8.24:1.2), and Dhammika (Snp 2.14:1.3).
sn55.53:2.2: Such discourses, which are also referred to at AN 2.47:1.5, AN 5.79:5.2, and SN 20.7:2.4, contrast with the frivolous poetry of outsiders. I understand the expression as referring to the Suttas in general, rather than specifying particularly difficult texts. | The expression “undertake and dwell” (upasampajja viharati) is normally used for meditation states, whereas for the Suttas one is enjoined to listen, scrutinize, and memorize. Perhaps the original intent was to “enter and dwell in the meditations taught in the Suttas”. | The Chāndogya Upaniṣad uses the Sanskrit form upasampadya for “entering the light (of the Self)” (8.3.4, 8.12.2–3). Pañcaviṁśabrāhmaṇa 13.10.16 uses it in the context of texts, but in a different way: “The two feet of the jagatī meter are subsumed in the gāyatrī.”
sn55.53:2.5: Given that Dhammadinna was evidently a sincere devotee, it seems odd that he should find studying or listening to Suttas from time to time to be impossible. After all, he is right now in the presence of the Buddha, listening to a Sutta. This, I think, lends credence to the notion that the Buddha was in fact talking about deep meditation.
